flawed_step: The first necessary exchange step is unjustified: a shortest interval can conflict with two mutually non-overlapping intervals, so inserting it into an optimal schedule may reduce the schedule size.
counterexample: Take A=[0,3), B=[3,7), and C=[2,4), with distinct durations 3, 4, and 2. The unique shortest interval is C, so every tie-breaking rule selects C first. C intersects A on [2,3) and B on [3,4), so the greedy algorithm discards both and returns only {C}, of size 1. But A and B are non-overlapping because the intervals are half-open and A ends exactly when B starts; hence {A,B} is a schedule of size 2. No schedule can have size 3 because C conflicts with both A and B, so the optimum is exactly 2.
assessment_summary: The proposed shortest-duration greedy rule returns 1 interval on the explicit instance, while the optimum returns 2. Thus the universal statement is false, with failure independent of tie-breaking.
